text: If you ever find yourself saying something like, that's not my job, that's probably a thing you should do. And you know what?
speaker: Maggie Crowley
context: Lenny asks Maggie about the common threads she's seen across the best product managers she's worked with, hired, and managed. Maggie explains her third key trait, which she calls 'carrying the water' - being willing to do the unglamorous work that needs to get done regardless of whose official responsibility it is. She emphasizes that PMs who succeed are those who focus on getting work done rather than getting frustrated about job boundaries.
text_ko: 혹시 '그건 제 일이 아니에요'라고 말하는 자신을 발견한다면, 그 일은 오히려 당신이 해야 할 일일 가능성이 커요. 그리고 있잖아요?
text_zh: 如果你发现自己会说“那不是我的工作”，那很可能正是你该做的事。你知道吗？
text_es: Si alguna vez te sorprendes diciendo "eso no es mi trabajo", probablemente sea justo lo que deberías hacer. ¿Y sabes qué?
key_sentence: that's probably a thing you should do.
original_text: If you ever find yourself saying something like, that's not my job, that's probably a thing you should do. And you know what? It probably isn't your job and it probably is someone else's job and you can spend your life getting frustrated at that or you can just get over and get the work done. And people who are willing to just get the work done will move faster. Their products will be more successful and they probably aren't carrying around all that anger and crappy emotion.

text: you're oftentimes the emotional center of the team and it's your job to keep people motivated, keep people excited, keep them bought into the project, and you just have to keep that optimism going.
speaker: Maggie Crowley
context: Lenny asks Maggie about the common threads across successful product managers. Maggie is explaining the concept of 'carrying the water' as a PM - being willing to do work that technically isn't your job. She describes how PMs often serve as the emotional center of their teams, responsible for maintaining team morale and motivation while also being willing to jump into any role needed to ensure project success.
text_ko: 여러분은 보통 팀에서 감정적 중심이 되는 경우가 많아요. 팀원들이 동기부여를 잃지 않고 계속 흥미를 느끼며 프로젝트에 진심으로 몰입하게 만드는 게 여러분의 역할이에요. 그리고 그 낙관적인 분위기를 계속 이어가야 해요.
text_zh: 你很多时候是团队的情绪中心，你的工作就是让大家有干劲、保持热情、继续认同并投入这个项目，而且你得一直把这种乐观情绪维持下去。
text_es: A menudo eres el centro emocional del equipo, y te toca mantener a la gente motivada, entusiasmada y comprometida con el proyecto; tienes que seguir transmitiendo ese optimismo.
key_sentence: you're oftentimes the emotional center of the team and it's your job to keep people motivated, keep people excited, keep them bought into the project
original_text: Because as a PM, for better or for worse, and maybe this is not how we all want it to be, but you're oftentimes the emotional center of the team and it's your job to keep people motivated, keep people excited, keep them bought into the project, and you just have to keep that optimism going and it's hard work and part of it can be just like, you know what? Let me take that on. I'll do this thing. I'll hop on this sales call, I'll implement this with the customer. You just have to do whatever it takes.

vocabulary.definition: Driven to take action or achieve goals, often fueled by personal ambition or external incentives.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, being motivated is crucial for employees to meet targets, enhance productivity, and contribute positively to team dynamics.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'motivated' generally has a positive connotation, it can imply pressure or stress if the motivation stems from external demands rather than personal desire.

vocabulary.definition: A hopeful and positive outlook on future outcomes, often leading to proactive behavior.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups and business, optimism can foster innovation and resilience, encouraging teams to pursue ambitious projects despite uncertainties.
vocabulary.nuance: While optimism is generally seen as beneficial, excessive optimism can lead to unrealistic expectations and poor decision-making.

vocabulary.definition: To accept or adopt an idea, plan, or project, often implying a commitment to its success.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, having team members 'bought into' a project is essential for collaboration and achieving collective goals, as it fosters a sense of ownership and accountability.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase often conveys a deeper level of commitment than simply agreeing with an idea; it suggests emotional and intellectual investment.

vocabulary.definition: The focal point of emotional support and motivation within a group, often responsible for influencing the morale and cohesion of the team.
vocabulary.businessContext: In team dynamics, being the emotional center means facilitating communication, resolving conflicts, and ensuring a positive work environment, which is vital for maintaining productivity.
vocabulary.nuance: While being the emotional center can be a strength, it may also lead to burnout if the individual feels solely responsible for the team's emotional well-being.

text: So many people in the spec or the one pager or something will say, okay, here's the metric that I care about. Here's what I want to move. Awesome.
speaker: Maggie Crowley
context: Lenny asks Maggie about the three traits that make great product managers. Maggie is explaining her second trait: following up on results. She describes how many PMs set metrics and track them initially, but the exceptional ones remember to circle back and report on what actually happened with their launches and initiatives, which is surprisingly rare and highly valued by leadership.
text_ko: 스펙(spec)이나 원페이저(one-pager) 같은 문서에 많은 사람들이 “제가 신경 쓰는 지표(metric)는 이거고, 이걸 움직이고 싶어요”라고 적어놔요. 좋아요.
text_zh: 很多人在需求文档（spec）或一页总结（one pager）之类的文档里会说，“好，这是我关心的指标，这是我想去推动的。太好了。”
text_es: Mucha gente, en la especificación (spec) o en un resumen de una página (one pager) o algo así, dirá: “vale, ésta es la métrica que me importa. Esto es lo que quiero mover. Genial.”
key_sentence: Here's the metric that I care about. Here's what I want to move.
original_text: So many people in the spec or the one pager or something will say, okay, here's the metric that I care about. Here's what I want to move. Awesome. Maybe they'll even write a SQL query, get a dashboard going, figure out what the number is today, that gets you some extra points, but the really, really good PMs remember to follow up. Because especially when you're in management, couple layers up in management, I'm not going to remember to follow up on that feature, but if a PM comes back to me and says, 'Hey, remember we did that thing, here's what happened.' I can't tell you how rare that is and how many times as a leader you might have to ask for that and for the people you don't have to ask that of is one of the best things when I'm looking at PMs and it's easy.

vocabulary.definition: A standard of measurement used to assess performance, progress, or quality in a specific area.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, metrics are crucial for evaluating the success of strategies and initiatives, often guiding decision-making processes.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'metric' often refers to quantitative measures, it can also imply a broader framework for assessing qualitative aspects, making it essential to clarify the context in which it is used.

text: Those things to me, communication, super important, analytical ability, really, really important.
speaker: Maggie Crowley
context: Lenny points out that Maggie's three traits for great PMs are different from the typical answers people give (communication, collaboration, vision, strategy). Maggie responds by distinguishing between what she considers the basics of being a PM versus what makes someone truly great at the role. She argues that while skills like communication and analytical thinking are important fundamentals, her three traits are what separate good PMs from great ones.
text_ko: 저한테는 의사소통(communication)이 엄청 중요하고, 분석 능력(analytical ability)도 정말 정말 중요해요.
text_zh: 对我来说，沟通很重要，分析能力真的至关重要。
text_es: Para mí, la comunicación es súper importante y la capacidad analítica, de verdad, es clave.
key_sentence: communication, super important, analytical ability, really, really important.
original_text: Those things to me, communication, super important, analytical ability, really, really important. The ability to look at a, especially if you're doing something that has a user experience component, the ability to look at that and understand if it's going to work and build up intuition around that, also really important. Those are things that I would see as sort of basics of the role. These are the things that make you great at the role and strategy to me, and hopefully we'll talk about strategy in a bit. It's one tiny slice. You do a strategy, but it's 5% of the work that you do.

vocabulary.definition: The capacity to systematically evaluate information, identify patterns, and draw logical conclusions based on data analysis.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, analytical ability is crucial for problem-solving, decision-making, and optimizing processes based on quantitative insights.
vocabulary.nuance: This term often implies a strong logical reasoning skill and is typically used in contexts where data-driven decision-making is emphasized.

vocabulary.definition: The act of conveying information effectively through verbal, non-verbal, or written means to ensure understanding between parties.
vocabulary.businessContext: Effective communication is vital in business environments for team collaboration, client relations, and stakeholder engagement, impacting overall organizational success.
vocabulary.nuance: While it generally refers to the exchange of information, it can also imply the quality and clarity of that exchange, making it essential to distinguish between mere transmission and effective communication.

text: People who are really excited about being data-driven... that says that the team is over-emphasizing quantitative data at the expense of qualitative data... they probably don't do a lot of direct user research... they don't really understand the humans who are using the thing.
speaker: Maggie Crowley
context: Lenny asks Maggie about contrarian opinions she holds about product management. Maggie shares her view that when people or executives emphasize being 'data-driven,' it often signals poor product thinking. She explains that this typically means teams are over-relying on quantitative metrics while neglecting qualitative insights from user research and losing touch with the actual humans using their products.
text_ko: 데이터 중심(data-driven)에 너무 신나하는 사람들은, 팀이 정량적 데이터(quantitative data)를 지나치게 강조하면서 정성적 데이터(qualitative data)를 소홀히 하고 있다는 얘기예요. 아마 직접 사용자 조사(direct user research)를 많이 안 하고, 그걸 실제로 사용하는 사람들(사용자)을 제대로 이해하지 못하는 경우가 많아요.
text_zh: 那些特别热衷于“数据驱动”(data-driven)的人，往往说明团队把定量数据 (quantitative data) 看得太重，忽视了定性数据 (qualitative data)。他们很可能没怎么做直接的用户研究 (direct user research)，也不太了解真正使用这个产品的人。
text_es: Las personas que están muy entusiasmadas con ser orientadas por los datos (data-driven) suelen poner demasiado énfasis en los datos cuantitativos a costa de los cualitativos; probablemente no hagan mucha investigación directa con usuarios (user research) y, por eso, no entienden realmente a las personas que usan su producto.
key_sentence: the team is over-emphasizing quantitative data at the expense of qualitative data
original_text: The one I like to have in this area is that people who are really excited about being data-driven, to me that is oftentimes a red flag for their product thinking, especially if it's an executive who's saying things like, oh, so we make all our decisions with our dashboards. To me that says that the team is over-emphasizing quantitative data at the expense of qualitative data and they're not using good judgment. They probably don't do a lot of direct user research. They don't really understand the humans who are using the thing, what they need, what they care about, and they're managing via a dashboard.

vocabulary.definition: Based on the analysis and interpretation of data rather than intuition or personal experience.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, being data-driven implies making decisions grounded in quantitative analysis to enhance performance and outcomes.
vocabulary.nuance: While being data-driven is generally seen as a positive approach, it can imply a neglect of qualitative insights if not balanced properly.

vocabulary.definition: Placing excessive importance or focus on a particular aspect, often to the detriment of other elements.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, over-emphasizing certain data types can lead to skewed decision-making and a lack of holistic understanding.
vocabulary.nuance: This term often carries a negative connotation, suggesting that balance is necessary for effective analysis.

vocabulary.definition: Information that is descriptive and conceptual, often collected through interviews, observations, and open-ended surveys.
vocabulary.businessContext: Qualitative data is crucial in understanding user experiences and motivations, providing context that quantitative data alone cannot offer.
vocabulary.nuance: While qualitative data is invaluable for insights, it can be seen as less rigorous than quantitative data, which may lead to its undervaluation in certain analyses.

vocabulary.definition: The systematic study of target users to understand their needs, behaviors, and experiences with a product or service.
vocabulary.businessContext: User research is essential in product development and marketing, as it informs design decisions and enhances user satisfaction.
vocabulary.nuance: While user research is critical for user-centric design, it can sometimes be overlooked in favor of faster, data-driven approaches.

text: Really if you're going to make good content, you have to sanitize and frameworkize the thing that you're working on.
speaker: Maggie Crowley
context: Lenny asks Maggie about her contrarian opinions on product content, which is relevant since they both create content about product management. Maggie explains how creating good content requires distilling complex work into clean frameworks, but this can mislead readers into thinking that following frameworks is the goal rather than creating actual business impact. She argues this creates noise in the product management field.
text_ko: 정말 좋은 콘텐츠를 만들려면, 지금 다루고 있는 걸 먼저 정리·정제(sanitize)하고 프레임화(frameworkize)해서 틀을 잡아야 해요.
text_zh: 其实，要想做出好内容，就得先把素材清理干净（sanitize），再把它结构化（frameworkize）。
text_es: Si de verdad quieres hacer buen contenido, tienes que depurarlo (sanitize) y darle una estructura (frameworkize) a lo que estás trabajando.
key_sentence: you have to sanitize and frameworkize the thing that you're working on.
original_text: Really if you're going to make good content, you have to sanitize and frameworkize the thing that you're working on. And then slowly, I think for a lot of people who are reading it and looking at it, their thinking starts to become, well look how well I did this framework. Look how well I implemented this thing. And they lose touch with the point which is creating impact. And so all of this content makes it really noisy and then makes people think that, oh, if I just do these things that I'll get what I want.

vocabulary.definition: To make something clean and free from harmful substances or elements, often by removing or altering undesirable aspects.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, sanitizing often refers to refining data or content to ensure it is appropriate, secure, and compliant with regulations before sharing or publishing.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'sanitize' generally has a positive connotation of improving safety or quality, it can imply that the original content was flawed or problematic.

vocabulary.definition: To create or establish a structured framework or system around a concept, project, or process to enhance clarity and organization.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startup environments, frameworkizing is crucial for developing methodologies that guide project execution and decision-making, ensuring consistency and efficiency.
vocabulary.nuance: This term is often used informally and may be seen as jargon; it suggests a proactive approach to structuring ideas or processes.

vocabulary.definition: The information, material, or subject matter presented in various forms, such as text, images, or videos, intended for consumption by an audience.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the digital landscape, content is a critical asset for marketing, branding, and engagement strategies, driving customer interaction and loyalty.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'content' is a neutral term, it can imply varying levels of quality and relevance, depending on the context in which it is used.
